_meta.tool: Pet Behavior Decoder (id: PetBehaviorDecoder, full rename 2026-09-06; route/i18n prefix kept as pet-weirdness-decoder/pwd_ — see notes)
_meta.how_to_regression_diff: Re-run cases (npm run check:golden pet-weirdness-decoder). Diff for QUALITY not exact match: HTTP 200, no truncation. V2 REWRITE (2026-09-05) replaced likelihood-scored differentials, breed genetic-predisposition lists, arbitrary age-bucket rules, invented prevalence, fabricated community anecdotes, and behavior-modification timelines with plausible explanations grounded only in what was reported. FINAL GENERAL PROMPT CORRECTIONS pass (2026-09-06) added 20 general reasoning rules plus an INPUT INTEGRITY ledger-and-self-check, the most important being: contradictory input fields (a free-text description vs. a structured Duration/Frequency selection) must be surfaced as an unresolved conflict, never silently merged or averaged. See case 'contradictory-duration-frequency-vs-description' below — this is the tool's own permanent regression guard for that exact failure mode, reproducing the case the correction was written for almost verbatim. Also renamed the 1-5 slider from 'severity' to a 'how concerning did this seem to you?' concern rating throughout (never described as clinical severity or as 'progressing'), and 6 new outputGuard.prohibit/require categories were added matching the least mechanically-checkable of the new rules (arbitrary test periods, home-observation-as-proof-of-cause, breed-as-personality, checkbox-meaning-expansion, silently-merged contradictions, invented-new-problem-for-generic-advice). KNOWN NON-DETERMINISTIC EDGE CASE (observed, not fixed, tracked in tool-notes): when the v2 guard's repair pass removes a violation from one item of a string array (e.g. what_you_reported[5]=contradicted_supplied_fact), it can leave that array slot as an empty string rather than deleting the slot, since a repair can only rewrite a string leaf, not resize an array. The frontend now defensively filters empty/whitespace-only items out of every rendered list and copy-to-clipboard build (src/tools/PetBehaviorDecoder.js, renamed from PetWeirdnessDecoder.js in the full rename below) so this never shows as a blank bullet — this is a permanent, correct-either-way defensive fix and does not depend on that guard behavior ever occurring. FINAL OUTPUT CORRECTIONS pass (2026-09-06, same day): 18 more specific wording rules added after a live-judged read of real output — conflict precedence stated up front (not just explained after the fact), banned two specific phrase patterns verbatim ('even if he seems fine between episodes' — an invented reassuring negative; 'something feels off in his gut' — a narrated internal sensation), banned causal-chain language for a mere association, required consolidating overlapping possibilities to at most 3 truly distinct ones, required 'what to watch' and 'what would change the next step' to stay non-overlapping, required the recommendation to be stated directly instead of hedged ('a low threshold for calling your vet') when vet contact is the actual advice, and required action_level to match that actual recommendation (not softened to watch_closely once the answer already recommends contacting a vet). The first two bans needed a second, more forceful pass (an explicit 'BANNED, verbatim and in substance' framing) after the softer 'do not add X, such as EXAMPLE' phrasing let the exact banned phrases straight through in a live test; re-verified clean across 2 fresh runs after sharpening. FINAL DEFTBRAIN QUALITY PASS (2026-09-06, same day, fourth pass): 12 more rules from a live-judged read of a nighttime-yowling case with spay status, age, and a frequency-dropdown/free-text conflict all present at once — 'nothing obvious' must not read as medical concern ruled out (only 'no obvious emergency sign' is the honest boundary); a supplied fact (spay status, indoor/outdoor, breed, age) must materially explain THIS behavior before it's used in an explanation, never included as decorative color merely because it exists; no invented prevalence/age-comparison claims; a hypothesis must not harden into a specific invented event ('animals in the walls'); a quiet night is an observation, not evidence a trigger is intermittent; free-text-overrides-a-vaguer-dropdown must be stated explicitly, not silently applied; a hypothetical reassuring condition stays conditional, never asserted as already true; vocalization tone is one observation among several, never a rule-out; a low-risk experiment's outcome is evidence of coincidence, not a confirmed mechanism; never force a third explanation merely to fill the section; and action_level must match what the answer is actually telling the visitor to do (watch_closely vs. vet_contact_recommended). Two of the twelve needed a SECOND, sharper pass after live-testing the German/cat scenario twice: the arbitrary-waiting-period ban (existing 'NO ARBITRARY TEST PERIODS' rule used soft 'Avoid X' phrasing and the model produced 'several more weeks' — one of its own listed bad examples — anyway; fixed with the same 'BANNED, verbatim and in substance' framing that worked in the prior pass) and the free-text-frequency rule (initial wording permitted silently adopting the specific value; fixed by requiring the reconciliation be STATED, with an explicit 'indistinguishable from never having noticed the conflict' framing). KNOWN NON-DETERMINISTIC RESIDUAL (documented, not fully closed): even after the sharper 'BANNED, verbatim' phrasing, the arbitrary-waiting-period ban held in only 1 of 2 live re-test runs ('several more weeks' still appeared once) — both the generating call AND the v2 guard's checker missed it (the checker only sees the tool's promise + prohibit SLUG NAMES, not the full CORE_PROMPT rule text with its banned examples, so it can't reliably catch a phrase-level violation the generating prompt didn't suppress). This is a real limit of prompt-only phrase suppression against LLM stochasticity, not a bug to chase further with more text. FULL RENAME (2026-09-06, same day, fifth pass): the earlier 2026-09-05 rename was display-name-only (id/route/i18n prefix all kept as PetWeirdnessDecoder/pwd_). That left the URL unchanged, no redirect, stale filenames, and TOOL_IDS/TOOL_ALIASES/tool-og-slugs.json all still pointing at the old id — genuinely incomplete for a tool whose name the visitor now sees everywhere. Completed per audit/REWRITE-INSTALL-KIT.md §7, following the CrashPredictor/BeforeTheCrash precedent exactly: id changed to PetBehaviorDecoder in tools.js; src/tools/PetWeirdnessDecoder.js renamed to PetBehaviorDecoder.js (component name + displayName updated, pickExample's localStorage key deliberately left as the old name); backend/server.js TOOL_IDS swapped (old id removed so it doesn't 301 to itself first) and LEGACY_REDIRECTS gained 3 real 301 entries (PascalCase, lowercase, kebab-case) for the old URL; TOOL_ALIASES in ToolRenderer.js gained the client-side fallback; tool-og-slugs.json and the public/og/og-slug-map.json mirror both gained a new-id entry (old entry kept alongside, unlike the CrashPredictor precedent which left NO new-id entry at all — a gap this rename does not repeat); scripts/localization-audit.js's LOCALIZED_TOOLS allowlist path updated to the new filename; the 6 guides/pets/*.js source files' toolId field (not just toolName, already fixed in the prior pass) updated, regenerating all cross-ref hrefs; DemoCards.js and HomeIntro.js's id references (both actually looked up against tools.js — a stale id here silently drops the tool from that surface) updated. Backend route file, i18n locale filename, and the pwd_ prefix all deliberately KEPT — internal, renaming them buys nothing and breaks saved state, exactly per the checklist's own explicit guidance and the CrashPredictor/BeforeTheCrash precedent (its i18n/backend files are still named crash-predictor.js). Verified with real HTTP status codes against the running server per the checklist's own instruction, not by reasoning about the dev SPA.

input.behavior: For the past week she's been yowling at 3am, running laps around the apartment, and knocking things off shelves. She's spayed and indoor-only. Nothing in the environment has changed.
input.whenItHappens: Mostly around 3am, then she settles down after 15-20 minutes.

assessment.headline: Nächtliches Jaulen und Umherlaufen gegen 3 Uhr
assessment.bottom_line: Auf Basis des Berichteten klingt dies nach einem erklärbaren nächtlichen Aktivitätsmuster, das bei Katzen vorkommen kann. Da es neu ist und regelmäßig auftritt, lohnt es sich, die Situation im Auge zu behalten – vor allem um sicherzustellen, dass keine körperliche Ursache dahintersteckt.

what_you_reported: Weibliche, kastrierte, 4 Jahre alte Hauskatze, ausschließlich Wohnungskatze.
Seit etwa einer Woche: lautes Jaulen, Spurts durch die Wohnung und Dinge von Regalen stoßen – hauptsächlich gegen 3 Uhr nachts.
Die Episoden dauern jeweils 15–20 Minuten, danach beruhigt sie sich wieder.
Laut Angabe keine Veränderungen in der Umgebung, Ernährung, Medikation oder Gesundheit.
Keine früheren gespeicherten Beobachtungen dieses Verhaltens vorhanden.
Dauer wurde als 'Wochen' angegeben, die Beschreibung nennt jedoch 'die letzte Woche' – ein leichter Widerspruch, der nicht aufgelöst wurde.

what_could_explain_it.possibility: Gesteigerter nächtlicher Bewegungsdrang ohne erkennbaren äußeren Auslöser
what_could_explain_it.why_it_could_fit: Katzen haben natürlicherweise Phasen erhöhter Aktivität, insbesondere in den frühen Morgenstunden. Bei einer reinen Wohnungskatze können solche Aktivitätsausbrüche mit Vokalisierung auftreten.
what_would_make_it_more_or_less_plausibl: Plausibler, wenn die Episoden sich auf Zeiten konzentrieren, in denen die Katze typischerweise aktiver ist.
Weniger naheliegend, wenn die Episoden intensiver werden, länger andauern oder von Anzeichen von Unruhe oder Schmerz begleitet sind.
Ein Versuch mit einer aktiven Spielsession am frühen Abend kann zeigen, ob sich das Muster dadurch verändert.

what_could_explain_it.possibility: Reaktion auf etwas außerhalb der Wohnung, das die Katze wahrnimmt
what_could_explain_it.why_it_could_fit: Geräusche, Gerüche oder Bewegungen – etwa andere Tiere im Treppenhaus oder draußen – könnten die Katze zu dieser Uhrzeit aktivieren, auch wenn die Besitzerin nichts bemerkt.
what_would_make_it_more_or_less_plausibl: Plausibler, wenn die Episoden immer in der Nähe von Fenstern, Türen oder Wänden zu Nachbarwohnungen stattfinden.
Weniger naheliegend, wenn die Katze völlig wahllos durch alle Räume läuft ohne Richtungsbezug.
Beobachten, ob Zugluft, Lichtveränderungen oder saisonale Faktoren (z. B. Tiere im Innenhof) mit dem Beginn zusammenpassen.

what_could_explain_it.possibility: Körperliche Ursache, die Unwohlsein oder veränderte Wahrnehmung auslöst
what_could_explain_it.why_it_could_fit: Neu auftretendes, regelmäßiges Jaulen kann in seltenen Fällen mit körperlichen Veränderungen zusammenhängen – ein Grund, dies mit der Tierärztin oder dem Tierarzt zu besprechen.
what_would_make_it_more_or_less_plausibl: Erhärtet sich, wenn gleichzeitig Veränderungen in Fress-, Trink- oder Toilettenverhalten auftreten, das Fell schlechter wird oder die Katze tagsüber weniger aktiv oder schlechter ansprechbar ist.
Auch relevant, wenn die Episoden häufiger oder intensiver werden statt gleich zu bleiben.
Kein Änderungshinweis wurde bisher berichtet – das ist nützliche Information, schließt eine körperliche Ursache aber nicht aus.

what_to_watch: Veränderungen beim Fressen, Trinken oder bei der Nutzung der Katzentoilette.
Ob die Episoden häufiger, länger oder intensiver werden.
Ob die Katze tagsüber weniger aktiv, weniger ansprechbar oder weniger an Spiel interessiert ist als sonst.
Ob sich die Qualität des Jaulens verändert – zum Beispiel ob es intensiver, häufiger oder anders strukturiert wird als bisher beobachtet.
Ob die Episoden beginnen, auch zu anderen Tageszeiten aufzutreten.
what_would_change_the_next_step: Gleichzeitige Veränderungen in Fress-, Trink- oder Ausscheidungsverhalten.
Das Jaulen klingt anhaltend, klagend oder anders als die kurzen Laute bei Spielaktivität.
Die Episoden werden in wenigen Tagen deutlich häufiger oder länger.
Die Katze wirkt tagsüber verändert – weniger reagierend, weniger aktiv oder körperlich anders.
what_you_can_do_now: Zeitpunkt, Dauer und Verlauf jeder Episode kurz notieren – das hilft, Muster zu erkennen und ist nützlich für ein mögliches Tierarztgespräch.

Falls die Episoden sich in den nächsten Tagen nicht verändern oder zunehmen, ist ein Gespräch mit der Tierärztin oder dem Tierarzt sinnvoll – um eine körperliche Ursache auszuschließen und Änderungen in Verhalten oder Gesundheit fachlich einzuordnen.
Prüfen, ob zur fraglichen Uhrzeit in der unmittelbaren Umgebung (Treppenhaus, Innenhof, Fenster) etwas vor sich geht, das die Katze aktivieren könnte.

what_to_record: Datum und Uhrzeit jeder Episode, Dauer und ungefähre Intensität.
Ob und welche begleitenden Veränderungen im Fress-, Trink- oder Toilettenverhalten auftreten.
Ein kurzes Video einer Episode, falls möglich – hilfreich für die Tierärztin oder den Tierarzt.
questions_or_details_to_bring: Seit wann genau das Verhalten aufgetreten ist und ob es sich verändert hat.
Ob es wirklich keine Umgebungsveränderungen gab – auch kleinere wie neue Möbel, andere Besuchsmuster oder Gerüche.
Wann die letzte allgemeine Untersuchung stattgefunden hat.

cases.name: spay-status-and-frequency-conflict-not-used-as-color
cases.why_this_case_exists: Permanent regression guard for the FINAL DEFTBRAIN QUALITY PASS (2026-09-06). Three things at once: a frequency-dropdown ('Occasionally') that conflicts with a clearly more specific free-text account ('nightly'), an emergency-adjacent bottom line that must not read as medical concern ruled out, and a supplied spay/indoor status that must NOT be used as decorative explanatory color. The output must (1) explicitly state the free-text-overrides-dropdown reconciliation in what_you_reported rather than silently applying it, (2) say 'no obvious emergency sign' rather than implying medical causes were checked and cleared, and (3) never use spay/indoor status to explain the behavior unless it actually does.

input.behavior: For the past two weeks she has been yowling loudly and running around the apartment nightly, mostly around 3am. She is spayed and indoor-only. Nothing in the environment has changed that I know of.
input.whenItHappens: Mostly around 3am, settles down after 15-20 minutes.

assessment.headline: Nightly yowling and activity bursts around 3am, ongoing two weeks
assessment.bottom_line: Based on what you reported, there is no obvious emergency sign, and the pattern you described can fit ordinary feline nighttime activity. Because it has been consistent for two weeks and includes loud vocalizing, it is worth tracking closely and mentioning to your vet if it continues or any new changes appear.

what_you_reported: Your cat has been yowling loudly and running around the apartment nightly for approximately two weeks.
Episodes happen around 3am and settle on their own after 15-20 minutes.
You described frequency as occasional, but your free-text description says this happens nightly — the more specific nightly description is used here.
She is 4 years old, spayed, and indoor-only.
No medications, recent diet changes, or health changes were reported.
You noted no environmental changes that you are aware of.

what_could_explain_it.possibility: Heightened nighttime activity that happens to cluster around the same hour
what_could_explain_it.why_it_could_fit: Cats can have bursts of active, vocal behavior at night, and a consistent time each night is something some cats do.
what_would_make_it_more_or_less_plausibl: More plausible if daytime activity, appetite, litter-box use, and interaction all remain unchanged.
Less straightforward if the vocalizing sounds distressed or pained rather than energized, or if episodes are getting longer or more intense.

what_could_explain_it.possibility: A response to something in or around the environment that has not been identified
what_could_explain_it.why_it_could_fit: Indoor cats can react to sounds, smells, or activity outside the apartment that an owner may not notice, particularly late at night when surroundings are quieter.
what_would_make_it_more_or_less_plausibl: Worth considering if the episodes seem to start in or near a window, door, or specific room.
Less likely to be the main factor if the behavior happens throughout the apartment with no consistent starting point.

what_could_explain_it.possibility: An underlying physical issue contributing to nighttime distress
what_could_explain_it.why_it_could_fit: Persistent nightly vocalizing that is new and consistent over two weeks can sometimes accompany a medical change, even when no other signs are obvious.
what_would_make_it_more_or_less_plausibl: Worth considering more seriously if appetite, drinking, litter-box habits, or daytime demeanor change.
Also worth considering if the vocalizing sounds painful or distressed rather than active.

what_to_watch: Whether the vocalizing sounds distressed or painful rather than energized.
Any change in appetite, drinking, or litter-box use.
Whether episodes are getting longer, louder, or more frequent.
Whether daytime behavior, activity level, or interaction with you changes.
Whether episodes seem to start in a specific location in the apartment.
what_would_change_the_next_step: The vocalizing starts sounding painful or distressed, or she seems uncomfortable during or between episodes.
Appetite, drinking, or litter-box habits change.
The pattern becomes noticeably more intense or frequent.
Any new physical sign appears — vomiting, limping, hiding, or changes in grooming.
what_you_can_do_now: Note briefly each morning whether an episode occurred and how it seemed — this record will be useful if a vet visit becomes appropriate.

If she seems interested in play in the evening, you could try an interactive play session before your usual bedtime and observe whether the nighttime pattern changes on the next few opportunities. This is an experiment to note, not a guaranteed fix.
Check whether episodes seem to start near a window or door, which could help you determine whether something outside may be a factor.

what_to_record: Whether an episode occurred each night, and roughly how long it lasted.
Whether the vocalizing sounds different from her usual voice — louder, more urgent, or distressed.
Any changes in eating, drinking, litter-box use, or daytime behavior.
questions_or_details_to_bring: When the episodes started and how consistently they occur.
Whether any recent changes — diet, environment, routine — preceded the start, even if they seem unrelated.
Whether her last wellness exam included bloodwork, in case baseline values would be useful to compare.

input.behavior: He's started eating grass obsessively on every walk, then vomiting within an hour. It's happened 4 times this week.
input.whenItHappens: Right after walks, within an hour.

assessment.headline: Repeated grass eating followed by vomiting, with reduced appetite and tiredness
assessment.bottom_line: Four vomiting episodes in one week, combined with eating less and lower energy, is enough to warrant a veterinary conversation soon — particularly because these changes are happening in a 9-year-old dog already on a daily medication.

what_you_reported: Grass eating on every walk, followed by vomiting within an hour, four times this week.
The pattern has been going on for about a week and is happening multiple times daily.
He is eating less at meals than usual.
He seems more tired than usual.
He is a 9-year-old Labrador mix currently taking Rimadyl (carprofen) for joint pain.
No recent diet changes or vet visits were reported.

what_could_explain_it.possibility: An underlying GI issue prompting the grass eating and vomiting
what_could_explain_it.why_it_could_fit: Dogs sometimes eat grass when experiencing stomach discomfort, and a recurring GI problem could explain both the vomiting and the reduced appetite. The tiredness could accompany that discomfort.
what_would_make_it_more_or_less_plausibl: More plausible if the vomiting also happens on days when grass eating is prevented, or if his stool has changed in consistency, color, or frequency.
Worth noting either way: whether he seems uncomfortable or restless before or after vomiting, beyond just the grass eating itself.

what_could_explain_it.why_it_could_fit: Carprofen can cause stomach upset, reduced appetite, and vomiting in some dogs, and these symptoms starting around the same time would be worth raising with the prescribing vet — not to stop the medication on your own, but to flag the timing.
what_would_make_it_more_or_less_plausibl: More worth exploring if the dosing schedule or anything about how it's given changed around the time this started.
The prescribing vet is better placed than this tool to weigh the medication's role, given they know his full history.

what_could_explain_it.possibility: Something encountered on walks contributing to the pattern
what_could_explain_it.why_it_could_fit: If the grass he's eating has been treated with a lawn chemical, or if he's picking up something else alongside it, that could be causing the vomiting rather than the grass itself.
what_would_make_it_more_or_less_plausibl: More plausible if the episodes are concentrated after walks in a specific area rather than all locations.
Worth checking whether the grass areas he favors could have been recently treated.

what_to_watch: Any vomiting that contains blood, or stool that is dark, tarry, or bloody — contact a vet promptly if this appears.
Whether the reduced appetite continues or he stops eating altogether.
Whether the tiredness increases or he becomes reluctant to move.
Whether vomiting occurs on a day when grass eating is prevented — this would be useful information for the vet.
what_would_change_the_next_step: Blood in vomit or stool, or black/tarry stool — these warrant urgent veterinary contact, not a routine appointment.
Vomiting that becomes more frequent, more forceful, or persists beyond what you have already described.
He stops eating entirely or shows signs of significant distress such as restlessness, hunching, or a distended abdomen.
A noticeable further drop in energy beyond what you have already noticed.
what_you_can_do_now: Contact the vet who prescribed Rimadyl and describe the full picture: the vomiting frequency, the reduced appetite, the tiredness, and how long it has been going on. Bring up the Rimadyl specifically so they can factor in the medication context.

On upcoming walks, note whether the grass eating and vomiting happen in the same locations each time, and whether preventing grass eating on one walk changes the pattern — this observation could help the vet.
Do not adjust or stop the Rimadyl on your own; that decision belongs with the prescribing vet given his joint condition.

what_to_record: The date and time of each vomiting episode and whether grass eating preceded it.
How much he is eating at meals relative to his usual amount.
Any change in his stool — consistency, color, frequency.
Whether the episodes happen on walks in specific locations or everywhere.
questions_or_details_to_bring: His current Rimadyl dose, how long he has been on it, and whether anything about when or how he takes it has changed recently.
Whether these GI signs could be related to the Rimadyl, and if so, what the options are.
Whether any exam or baseline bloodwork would be appropriate given his age and these new symptoms.

cases.name: contradictory-duration-frequency-vs-description
cases.why_this_case_exists: Permanent regression guard for the FINAL GENERAL PROMPT CORRECTIONS pass (2026-09-06). The free-text description says the episode happened 'four times this week' while the structured Duration field says 'Just started today' and Frequency says 'Multiple times daily' — three fields that cannot all literally be true together. Before this pass the model silently merged them into one smoothed-over story. It must now surface the conflict plainly in what_you_reported, state which account it is relying on, and reason from that — never guess silently and never pretend all three fields agree.

input.behavior: He keeps eating grass outside and then vomiting afterward. It has happened four times this week.

assessment.headline: Repeated grass eating followed by vomiting, four times this week
assessment.bottom_line: Four vomiting episodes in one week is worth taking seriously even without other changes reported. Based on what you described, this doesn't point clearly to an emergency, but the frequency means it's worth watching closely and contacting your vet if the pattern continues or anything else changes.

what_you_reported: Your 2-year-old Labrador mix has eaten grass and vomited afterward four times this week.

A note on timing: the Duration field says 'just started today,' but you also described four episodes this week — these can't both be literally true. The assessment is based on four episodes this week as the more specific detail; if the episodes all happened today, that increases urgency.
No other changes were reported: no medications, no recent diet or health changes, no selected associated changes.
No information was provided about what happens before, during, or after the episodes.

what_could_explain_it.possibility: Grass eating as a response to GI discomfort, with vomiting as a result
what_could_explain_it.why_it_could_fit: Dogs sometimes eat grass when something in the GI tract is off, and vomiting can follow. Four episodes in a week could suggest an ongoing GI issue rather than a one-time event.
what_would_make_it_more_or_less_plausibl: Whether he seems uncomfortable, unsettled, or is licking his lips before seeking grass
Whether vomiting also happens at times when grass isn't involved
Whether stool consistency or appetite has changed, even if not yet reported

what_could_explain_it.possibility: Grass eating as a habit or self-directed behavior, with vomiting as an incidental outcome
what_could_explain_it.why_it_could_fit: Some dogs eat grass regularly without an obvious trigger, and vomiting sometimes follows without indicating an underlying problem. At 2 years old, this can occur without a medical cause.
what_would_make_it_more_or_less_plausibl: Whether he seems completely normal in energy, appetite, and comfort between episodes
Whether the vomiting always follows grass eating specifically, or happens at other times too
Whether the episodes stop if grass access is limited on a few walks

what_could_explain_it.possibility: Something encountered outdoors contributing to the episodes
what_could_explain_it.why_it_could_fit: If the grass is in an area treated with a lawn chemical, fertilizer, or pesticide, or if he's ingesting something mixed in with the grass, that could be relevant to both the eating behavior and the vomiting.
what_would_make_it_more_or_less_plausibl: Whether the episodes happen in one specific outdoor area or across different locations
Whether the grass has been recently treated with any lawn product
Whether anything else — stool changes, lethargy, drooling, or repeated attempts to vomit — has appeared alongside the vomiting

what_to_watch: Whether vomiting happens more than once on a single day, or the total number of episodes increases
Any change in appetite, stool consistency, or energy level
Signs of discomfort between episodes: restlessness, repeated lip-licking, reluctance to move, or a hunched posture
Whether vomiting occurs at times when grass was not involved
Any blood in the vomit or stool, or repeated unproductive retching
what_would_change_the_next_step: Vomiting becomes more frequent, or multiple episodes occur within a single day
Blood appears in the vomit or stool
He shows signs of distress, significant lethargy, or stops eating
Repeated unproductive retching or an obviously distended or rigid abdomen — contact a vet urgently if this happens
what_you_can_do_now: Note whether the episodes are happening in one specific outdoor area, and whether that area may have been treated with any lawn product recently.
On the next few walks, limiting grass access where practical and noting whether vomiting still occurs is a reasonable observation — if the pattern changes, that's useful information for your vet.
Keep a brief log: date, time, whether grass was eaten, and what the vomit looked like. Four episodes already makes a vet conversation reasonable; a log makes it more useful.
Contact your vet now if the episodes are all happening today rather than spread across the week — same-day repeated vomiting warrants a prompt call.

what_to_record: Date and time of each episode
Whether grass was definitely eaten beforehand, and roughly how much if you could tell
What the vomit looked like — whether it contained grass, was yellow or foamy, or had any blood
Any changes in appetite, stool, or energy you notice between now and the appointment
questions_or_details_to_bring: Whether the episodes are spread across several days or clustered on one or two days
Whether the outdoor areas involved could have been treated with lawn chemicals or fertilizers
Any recent diet, medication, or environmental changes, even ones that seemed minor

assessment.headline: Nighttime yowling and bursts of activity

output.answer:
The original analysis flagged 'new symptoms appear' as exactly the thing that would move you to the next step — so you're right to think about it. The key is noticing anything that feels different from the nighttime yowling and activity you've already been watching: things like changes in eating, drinking, litter box use, weight, coat condition, coordination, or any sign of pain or distress during the day.

If you notice something like that, the practical move is to write it down — what you saw, when, and how often — before contacting your vet. That record helps a lot more than memory alone.

One thing worth saying plainly: if you ever see something that looks urgent — collapse, labored breathing, inability to urinate, a seizure, or obvious pain — don't wait. That warrants a same-day or emergency call regardless of what came before. A new symptom doesn't automatically connect to the yowling, but it does deserve fresh attention on its own terms.
